back: provides data integrity, authentication, and data encryption so packets stay confidential over an unprotected network or the Internet. Originally built to avoid the cost of leased lines; now used for security and privacy.
tunnels between two or more network infrastructure devices at different sites, over a shared medium like the Internet. Common protocols are IPsec, GRE, and MPLS VPN.
lets users work from home, hotels, and other places as if directly connected to the corporate network. The tunnel runs between a VPN headend device and an end-user workstation or hardware VPN client.
legacy VPN protocol.
legacy VPN protocol with no integrity, authentication, or encryption.
tunneling protocol with no built-in security. Combined with IPsec as L2TP over IPsec.
IP protocol 47. Encapsulates packets of any protocol (the payload) inside any other protocol (the delivery protocol) between two endpoints. No security of its own.
provider VPN with no built-in integrity, authentication, or encryption.
the preferred VPN protocol because it provides integrity, authentication, and encryption. L2TP, GRE, and MPLS can be combined with IPsec to get these.
legacy protocol replaced by TLS. TLS-based VPNs are still called SSL VPNs.
created by the IETF to merge the vendor SSL versions into one open standard.

front: ISAKMP (Internet Security Association and Key Management Protocol)
back: the framework IKE runs in.
negotiates and establishes IPsec site-to-site and remote-access tunnels.
the original IKE. Two phases: Phase 1 (main mode or aggressive mode) and Phase 2 (quick mode).
the newer IKE. Simpler, more efficient exchanges, and fixes IKEv1 vulnerabilities.
the agreed set of security parameters between peers.
the secure channel that protects the Phase 2 negotiation.
one-way (unidirectional) SA that protects data. One negotiation always creates two, one inbound and one outbound.
unique value that identifies an SA. Each SA gets two SPIs, one from the initiator and one from the responder.
IKEv1 Phase 1 exchange of six packets in three round trips.
IKEv1 Phase 1 exchange of three packets.
IKEv1 Phase 2. Negotiates the IPsec SAs.

key agreement protocol used to derive a shared secret without sending it over the unsecured medium. The book also describes it as letting two devices "authenticate each other's pre-shared keys without actually sending the keys"; strictly, Diffie-Hellman agrees on keys and does not authenticate anything by itself (this clarification is not in the book).
defines the strength of the Diffie-Hellman exchange.
a string derived from secret material known only to the active participants. It keys the encrypted fifth and sixth main mode packets.
a randomly generated value sent with the Key Exchange payload.
carries the Diffie-Hellman public value.
newly generated keys are unrelated to any earlier key. Adds a new Diffie-Hellman calculation in Phase 2 instead of reusing Phase 1 keying.
IKEv2 only. Builds the keying material for all the algorithms used in the SAs.
the Phase 2 policy. Sets the encryption and hashing for data packets after the secure connection is up. Negotiated in quick mode. The name is only locally significant.
IP protocol 50. The book's text also writes it as "Encapsulation Security Payload" and "Encapsulated Security Payload". It is the default IPsec protocol.
IP protocol 51.
protects the upper-layer protocols (TCP, UDP). Used when the packets come from the VPN peers themselves, such as GRE over IPsec.
protects the entire IP packet. Used when packets come from hosts behind the VPN device. The default on Cisco IPsec devices.
IKEv2 Phase 1, made of the IKE_SA_INIT message pair. Its attributes are set in the Key Exchange Policy.
IKEv2 Phase 2. The first CHILD_SA is the IKE_AUTH message pair. Extra CHILD_SA pairs carry rekeys and informational messages. Its attributes are set in the data policy.
IKEv2 anti-DoS feature. Gives a session zero state while the gateway is under attack.
built into IKEv2. Detects a peer that has gone away.
built into IKEv2. Tells the peer to clear old SAs (the purpose is not in the book).
peers authenticate with a shared secret. Typical for small and medium organizations.
authentication with certificates. Used by large organizations for scale, central management, and extra security.
a standard that allows many authentication methods. Supported natively in IKEv2, not in IKEv1.
a PAT device builds its Layer 4 translation table from the SPI values, so ESP or AH can pass through.
peers detect a NAT or PAT device between them and wrap the packets in UDP 4500 so they can be translated.
periodic message that stops a NAT device from timing out the idle UDP 4500 entry.
the initiator and responder identities that say which traffic the CHILD_SA protects. Shown in Figure 8-7.
says which network, protocol, or port to encrypt. Can be anything from an entire network to one host and one port.
64 bits long per the book. Avoid; use AES. Only 56 of those bits are key bits (not in the book but worth knowing).
168 bits long. Avoid; use AES.
128 bits long.
192 and 256 bits long. AES 256 is recommended because its performance cost is about the same as weaker algorithms.
hashing algorithm. SHA-1 is recommended over MD5 for IKE because it is more secure and has fewer collisions.
older hashing algorithm.
stronger hashes for the ASA IPsec proposal. SHA-512 is the book's recommendation.
the keyed hash form used by ESP, as in esp-sha-hmac.

the ISAKMP Domain of Interpretation for group key management. Runs between a group member and the key server.

Cisco's IKEv2-based VPN framework. One CLI for point-to-point, remote-access, hub-and-spoke, and dynamic mesh. Does not rely on multipoint interfaces.
the headend and the IKEv2 initiator.
